summary: TLS handshake fails for large cert chains / OCSP staples over Direct Connect path (PMTU-related)
description:
Issue summary: Customer's Private deployment (Direct Connect) is failing TLS handshakes intermittently when the server certificate chain is large and includes an OCSP staple. Impact: model streaming connections fail to establish from the customer's on-prem network to Redwood private nodes; customers observe immediate TLS handshake termination and 5xx errors in our control plane logs.

Impact: Several production endpoints for NeuroDocs' clinical summarization pipeline are unable to connect to our runtime during peak hours; retries temporarily succeed when client reduces TLS max fragment size, but normal clients fail.

Environment: Private deployment over AWS Direct Connect (single DX link to us-east-1), customer-controlled on-prem firewall (hardware appliance), VPC route through TGW attachment to Redwood private node. TLS mTLS not used; server certificate chain includes an intermediate + long OCSP staple.

Observed behaviour:
- TLS handshake fails with 'unexpected_message' or 'handshake_failure' on client side.
- Redownloading with smaller MSS/MTU or enabling TCP MSS clamping at the edge allows handshake to complete.
- New TCP connections after MTU adjustment work; long-lived connections that require handshake renegotiation fail.

Hypothesis: Path MTU blackhole between customer on-prem and Redwood node causes larger TLS ServerHello/Certificate/OCSP responses to be dropped/fragmented and blocked by on-prem firewall, resulting in incomplete handshake and immediate teardown. The OCSP staple increases TLS record size above the PMTU, provoking fragmentation that intermediate gear drops.

Steps to reproduce:
1) From customer's on-prem network, initiate a TLS session to the private node on port 443 with default MTU.
2) Observe client logs showing handshake failure after ServerHello.
3) Lower client MTU or enable TCP MSS clamping on the on-prem firewall and repeat; handshake succeeds.

Logs and evidence:
- Client Wireshark capture (supplied by customer) showing TCP retransmits and fragmented TLS records around the large Certificate message.
- VPC flow logs show established TCP but no application-level ACKs for the large packet.
- Control plane logs: tls_handshake_error entries with TLS_ALERT 40 (handshake_failure) correlated to the customer's IP.
- On-prem firewall inspection log snippets (customer-supplied) showing 'fragmented packet dropped' for packets > 1400 bytes.

Temporary mitigation: Customer enabled TCP MSS clamping on their edge firewall (reduce MSS to 1360) which results in successful handshakes for affected endpoints. As a short-term workaround we suggested increasing MTU on Direct Connect jumbo support path (if available) or configure MSS clamp on the customer's appliance.

Next steps / tasks:
- Confirm exact PMTU along DX + TGW path using traceroute/MTU probes (ENG task assigned).
- Validate whether AWS Direct Connect or TGW attachment is doing any packet-size normalization that could interact with customer's firewall.
- Add a server-side config option in the private node agent to advertise smaller TCP MSS during the TLS handshake (investigate feasibility).
- Customer to provide deterministic pcap for packet-level proof (they already attached one).

Requested outcome: Permanent fix either by documenting PMTU requirements for Private Direct Connect paths and adding a note in the onboarding checklist, or by implementing server-side mitigations so large cert chains / OCSP staples do not fail on common enterprise firewalls.
steps_to_reproduce: From customer on-prem host, open TLS connection to private node (port 443) with default MTU
Observe client-side tls handshake failure (handshake_failure) after ServerHello when certificate + OCSP exceed PMTU

investigation_notes: 03-10: Initial triage by Support (Aisha) - customer provided pcap showing large TLS certificate bursts and immediate retransmits
03-11: Networking team (Jared) ran MTU probe across TGW and Direct Connect; probe shows drop at 1460 bytes in customer's appliance
03-12: Confirmed firewall vendor (AcmeEdge 9000) has fragmentation drop-by-default for non-DF-cleared fragments; customer appliance is dropping large fragments
03-13: Eng verified VPC and TGW attachments do not intentionally lower MTU; Direct Connect link is running standard 1500 MTU (no jumbo)
logs: customer-pcap: showing TLS Certificate record split across IP fragments, second fragment dropped by firewall
comments: 2026-03-10 | Aisha Patel (Support): Received initial report from NeuroDocs. Asked for pcap and firewall logs; provided by customer at 15:40 UTC.
2026-03-11 | Jared Kim (Network Eng): Ran MTU probing; initial indications point to packet drops when payload > 1460. Requesting the customer's firewall vendor and model to verify fragment handling.
2026-03-11 | Customer (NeuroDocs - ops@neurodocs.com): Confirmed appliance is AcmeEdge 9000 running firmware 4.2.0. They reported they default to dropping non-reassembled fragments for performance.
2026-03-12 | Jared Kim (Network Eng): Verified DX and TGW do not perform fragmentation. This is consistent with on-prem firewall blocking fragments — MSS clamp workaround validated by customer.
2026-03-13 | Aisha Patel (Support): Notified Customer Success that a policy doc and onboarding checklist should be updated to call out PMTU considerations for Direct Connect private deployments.
2026-03-14 | Jared Kim (Network Eng): Draft PR linked to infra repo to add optional MSS-clamp flag in private-node agent and documentation entry opened.
resolution: Mitigated via customer-side TCP MSS clamping (1360). Long-term actions in progress: 1) add documentation and onboarding checklist item for PMTU/fragmentation requirements for Private Direct Connect deployments; 2) engineering spike to add server-side MSS clamp / TLS record size mitigation in private-node agent (PR opened).
